title: Loops
summary: Do something many times without writing it many times.
refresher: A `for` **loop** repeats once for each item in a sequence. `for x in [1, 2, 3]:` runs the body three times, with x holding 1, then 2, then 3. To count instead, use `range(n)`, which stops just before n. A `while` loop keeps going as long as its **condition** is true, so something inside it has to eventually make that condition false. Otherwise it never stops.

blocks.body: A **loop** is how you tell the computer to do something again. Without one, printing the numbers 1 through 100 would mean writing 100 lines. With one, it takes two.

blocks.title: Trace a loop one item at a time
blocks.caption: Watch the active item move while the running total changes.

steps.title: Start before the loop
steps.body: The total starts at zero before any item is read.

steps.title: First pass
steps.body: Read index 0 and add 3 to the total.

steps.title: After the last item
steps.body: The loop stops after each item has contributed once.

blocks.caption: A `for` **loop** runs its body once for each item in a sequence. The sequence here is a **list** of three names, so the body runs three times.
blocks.output:
Hello, Ada
Hello, Grace
Hello, Alan

blocks.body: The **variable** after `for`, in this case `name`, is called the **loop** variable. You pick what to call it. On each pass it automatically holds the next item, so you never assign it yourself.

blocks.title: The indentation is the loop
blocks.body: In Python, the indented lines under `for` are the body of the **loop**. Un-indent a line and it is no longer inside the loop, so it runs once, after the loop has finished. This is the single most common cause of "why did it only **print** once?"

blocks.caption: To count rather than walk a **list**, use `range(n)`. It produces 0, 1, and so on, stopping just before n. `range(5)` therefore gives you five numbers: 0 through 4.

blocks.title: range(5) does not include 5
blocks.body: This catches almost everyone at least once. `range(5)` gives you 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. It stops before 5, never reaching it. If you want 1 through 5, write `range(1, 6)`. Getting this wrong by a single step is so common that it has its own name: an off-by-one error.

blocks.prompt: How many times does this **loop** **print**, and what is the last number it prints?
blocks.why: `range(4)` produces 0, 1, 2, 3. That is four numbers, and it stops before reaching 4. So the **loop** runs four times and the last thing printed is 3. If you picked "last number 4", you have just met the off-by-one error in person, which is the most useful way to meet it.

blocks.body: The other pattern worth knowing early is the accumulator. Start with an empty total, then add to it on each pass. Almost every problem that asks you to add things up, count how many, or build a **list** is really this pattern wearing a different hat.

blocks.caption: Notice that `total` is created before the **loop** starts. Create it inside and it would be reset to 0 on every pass, so the answer would always come out as just the last number.
blocks.code:
total = 0
for price in [4, 7, 2]:
    total = total + price
print(total)

blocks.body: A `while` **loop** works differently. It does not walk through a sequence. It simply keeps going for as long as its **condition** stays true, which makes it the right choice when you cannot know in advance how many repeats you will need.

blocks.caption: This counts down. The **condition** is checked before each pass, so once `n` reaches 0 the **loop** stops without running the body again.
blocks.code:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
print("Liftoff!")

blocks.caption: A `while` **loop** only ends if something inside it changes the **condition**. Leave that line out and the program hangs forever, because the loop has been given no reason to stop.
blocks.wrong:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
# n never changes,
# so n > 0 stays true
blocks.right:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
# n shrinks each pass,
# so n > 0 eventually fails

blocks.prompt: This **loop** is meant to count up to 5. What actually happens?
blocks.code:
count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
count = count + 1
blocks.why: Look at the indentation. `count = count + 1` sits outside the **loop** body, so it never runs while the loop is going. `count` stays at 1, the **condition** `count <= 5` stays true, and the loop prints 1 over and over. Indent that last line by four spaces and it works. Whenever a run of yours times out, this is the first thing to check.

blocks.title: If your code times out, suspect a while loop
blocks.body: An infinite **loop** is the usual reason a run never finishes. Ask yourself one question: what inside this loop will eventually make the **condition** false? If you cannot point at the line that does it, you have found your bug.

blocks.title: Which loop should I reach for?
items: You have a **list**, a **string**, or a range to walk through: use `for`
You know how many times to repeat: use `for` with `range(n)`
You repeat until something becomes true, and cannot say how long that takes: use `while`
When you are unsure, start with `for`. It cannot run forever.

for-count-01.title: Count loop passes
for-count-01.body: This asks how many times the loop body runs, not what the loop variable is used for.
for-count-01.notice: Count the values the loop produces, then count one body run per value.
for-count-01.mistake: Do not subtract one just because counting starts at zero.

off-by-one-01.title: Stop values are often excluded
off-by-one-01.body: A counting range usually stops before its stop value. That is the classic off-by-one place.
off-by-one-01.notice: List the first and last generated values before picking an output.
off-by-one-01.mistake: Do not include the stop boundary unless the syntax says it is included.

accumulator-01.title: Accumulators keep a running result
accumulator-01.body: A total starts before the loop and changes once per pass.
accumulator-01.notice: Write the total after each item to see the final value.
accumulator-01.mistake: Do not jump straight to the last item and forget earlier additions.

accumulator-reset-01.title: Initialize before the loop
accumulator-reset-01.body: A running total must be created outside the repeated body so it does not restart each pass.
accumulator-reset-01.notice: If a total keeps forgetting, check where it is initialized.
accumulator-reset-01.mistake: Do not put the reset line inside the loop unless each pass needs a fresh total.

while-infinite-01.title: A while loop needs progress
while-infinite-01.body: A while condition is checked again and again. Something in the body must eventually make it false.
while-infinite-01.notice: For timeouts, trace the condition variable after one pass.
while-infinite-01.mistake: Do not write a while loop that only prints and never updates the condition state.

while-countdown-01.title: The condition is checked before each pass
while-countdown-01.body: A countdown loop stops as soon as the condition becomes false, even if that final value looks important.
while-countdown-01.notice: Check whether the value is printed before or after the update.
while-countdown-01.mistake: Do not include the first value that fails the condition.

nested-count-01.title: Nested loops multiply work
nested-count-01.body: The inner loop runs fully for every outer-loop pass.
nested-count-01.notice: Multiply the number of outer passes by the number of inner passes for simple nested counts.
nested-count-01.mistake: Do not add the loop lengths when one loop is inside the other.

loop-body-scope-01.title: Indentation or braces decide the loop body
loop-body-scope-01.body: A line inside the loop runs every pass. A line after the loop runs once.
loop-body-scope-01.notice: Locate the output line before counting printed lines.
loop-body-scope-01.mistake: Do not assume a nearby line belongs to the loop if its block shape says otherwise.

range-start-01.title: Start and stop are different jobs
range-start-01.body: With a start and stop, the loop begins at the start value and still stops before the stop value.
range-start-01.notice: Write the sequence before choosing the output.
range-start-01.mistake: Do not include the stop value just because it appears in the range call.

count-matches-01.title: Counters update only on matching passes
count-matches-01.body: A counter with an `if` changes only when the condition is true.
count-matches-01.notice: Walk each item and mark yes or no before counting.
count-matches-01.mistake: Do not add one for every item when only qualifying items count.
